title: Developing (Learning) Skills - 1
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton sets out how skills differ from knowledge, framing knowledge as I know that and skills as I am able to. Across eight contrasts he shows that skills are variable in action, define what a person is, stay stable and few across time, need developmental assessment in action, and can only be learned in context. He adds that skill learning is personal and visible, takes long periods of practice, and depends on coaching rather than telling. Examples include bike riders of different ages, an eighteenth-century scientist in a modern lab, and his own failed attempt to learn skiing from a book. The argument is that confusing the two leads schools to teach, assess and give feedback on skills as if they were facts.
points: Skills are the evidence of being a musician, scientist or artist, whereas knowledge only shows what you know.
Core skills in a discipline are few and stable over centuries, unlike the ever-growing body of knowledge.
Skills must be assessed by watching them in action and judged against the learner's developmental level.
Skills learning is public and personal, takes long stretches of time, and requires coaching, so schools that treat skills like facts expect results they will not get.
quotes: Skills learning is about learning things that we are able to do. The starter sentence that identifies all of our skills learning is: ‘I am able to…’.

Skills are the difference between knowing music and being a musician; knowing science and being a scientist; knowing art and being an artist; knowing how to negotiate and being able to. Skills are the essential evidence that you are something. Knowledge isn’t.

These eight skills are at the heart of being a scientist. They were at the heart of being a scientist in the 18th century and they are at the heart of being a scientist in the 21st century. They are unlikely to change any time soon.

There’s far fewer places to hide in skills learning. That lack of hiding places may cause me to look good to others and feel good in myself. That same lack of hiding places may cause me to look incapable to others and/or increase my sense of embarrassment or shame.

He talks about how the Beatles were anything but an overnight success; it was their ’10000 hours’ in the clubs of Hamburg playing 12 hours a night for days on end that had them ready and hardwired - as musicians, as a band and as colleagues - to be able to take advantage when their big moment came. Overnight success at anything involving skills is anything but overnight if it is going to be truly sticky.

I know this sounds obvious but many of us - and many schools and curriculums - don’t give ourselves or our children the time we and they need to get better. We treat skills like knowledge and want almost instant results. We aren’t going to get them.

A coach is someone who reassures me that I’m on the right path, gives me time for my own practice, watches what is happening and, at the right time, steps in with some guidance. That book I bought - Learn to Ski in 48 Hours - didn’t work because it told me things (knowledge) but couldn’t coach me (skills).
